# So you want to write a compiler for BEES

**Status: draft, 2026-11-04.** This is the BEES target contract in its first form. It is for the author of **any**
language-to-Silica compiler, BEAM language or not: it states what your compiler must do for its output to run on BEES,
and what BEES provides in return. It is self-contained.

**It assumes your compiler is generated by an AI.** Read section 0 first.

Words used: **must** is a requirement. **may** is your choice. **open** means not decided yet: rely on neither
answer. **provisional** means it works today and is expected to change.

Verified so far on Apple Silicon macOS with Silica fixed point `silica-999939`. Other targets (Linux AArch64, Linux
x86-64, ESP32-S3) are planned and not yet verified.

---

## 0. If an AI generates your compiler

This document is written so that a generator can follow it without a human filling gaps.

- **Give the generator this whole document**, plus the BEES units listed in Part B and the conformance programs (A10).
  Treat the requirements as the specification and the conformance programs as the acceptance test.
- **Every requirement has an identifier** (A3.4, A6.9, and so on). Generated code, tests and the compiler's own
  documentation should cite them, so a reviewer can trace each lowering to the rule behind it.
- **Do not invent.** The generator may use only the Silica constructs it can verify against the Silica compiler and the
  BEES units named in Part B. A symbol, function or option that this document does not list does not exist. Where a
  requirement says **open**, the generator must stop and report the open point by identifier, not pick an answer.
- **The Silica compiler is the authority on what is legal.** Treat its error codes as ground truth; the codes cited here
  (for example E2236, E2237, E2008, E3010) are the ones met so far. When Silica rejects generated code, fix the
  generator, not the test.
- **Verify in a loop.** After each generation: run `bees_config check` on the output, build with the Silica compiler,
  run the conformance programs (`contract/conformance`), diff the output against the expected output, and check the
  lowering-choices file. A change is accepted only if all four pass.
- **Be deterministic.** The same source program must produce the same Silica source, the same unit basenames and the
  same manifests on every run, so the build and the goldens stay stable across regeneration.
- **Record every choice.** The compiler must produce a **lowering-choices file** (A9) listing, for each construct the
  contract leaves to you, which lowering it used. This is how a human reviews what the generator decided. Its format is
  defined in `contract/conformance/lowering-choices.md` and checked by `tools/check_lowering_choices.py`.
- **Keep a person in the loop for security.** Foreign-function code and anything that reads untrusted input (A8) must be
  reviewed by a person before it ships; a generator cannot certify its own security boundary.
- **Changes to Silica or to BEES themselves are outside this document.** If the generator concludes that Silica or BEES
  must change, it reports that as a proposal and does not work around it silently.

## 1. What BEES is, and what you are

BEES is a shim that sits between compiled programs and Silica. Your compiler turns source programs into Silica
source; the Silica compiler builds that together with BEES's units into a native program. Nothing is interpreted and
no bytecode is loaded.

- **Your compiler owns the language.** Everything Silica can already express, however awkwardly, you lower yourself.
  BEES adds only what Silica lacks (the value model, library services, exit tracking, distribution, balancing).
- **BEES does not narrow Silica.** Where Silica can do more than your language, your compiler may expose it.
- **BEES makes compilation possible, not easy.** It promises no fidelity to any particular language's semantics;
  fidelity is your compiler's business.

## 2. Terms

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Actor | A Silica actor: an isolated unit of work with a mailbox and private state, run one message at a time. |
| Dispatch | One message handled by an actor. Silica never interrupts a dispatch. |
| Value | A `bees_term`: the representation of any value that crosses a module, actor or network boundary. |
| Symbol | An interned name. In BEES it is a Silica atom. |
| Supervisor | A Silica supervisor actor that starts, restarts and ends child actors. |
| Listener, hub | The BEES FailureReporter and the BEES actor that records every actor's end. |

---

# Part A. What your compiler must do

## A1. Build and packaging

- **A1.1** Emit Silica source, one unit per module or generated helper. Every unit's basename must be unique across the
  whole program, and must start with a prefix reserved for your language. BEES's own units use `bees_` and
  `dangerous_bees_`.
- **A1.2** Emit, beside each unit, a **manifest** listing every symbol (Silica atom spelling) the unit uses, one per
  line (`<unit>.atoms`; `#` starts a comment). `bees_config generate` merges all manifests into one generated unit,
  `bees_atoms`, and also puts into it every symbol the module and pool manifests below name. Symbols must be
  identifiers (letters, digits and underscore, not starting with a digit); other spellings are not supported yet.
- **A1.3** Emit a **module manifest** for each module that can be called by name or through a function value
  (section A7): a line-oriented file `<unit>.module`, one module per file. Lines, in any order after the first:

  ```
  module <name>                 required, first: the module's name, a symbol spelling
  unit <silica_unit>            optional: the Silica unit holding the functions (default: the file's base name)
  entry <name> <arity> <fn>     an exported function <name>/<arity> (0 <= arity <= 255), implemented by Silica function <fn>
  fun <id> <fn>                 a function-value body with module-local id <id> (0 <= id < 2^31), implemented by <fn>
  ```

  `bees_config generate` reads every `.module` file and writes the unit `bees_modules` (A7). Within a module, an
  entry (name and arity) or a fun id may be listed only once; every module name must be unique in the program; the
  program may hold at most about one million symbols. `bees_config` rejects a manifest that breaks these rules with
  `file:line: message` and a non-zero exit.
- **A1.3a** Emit a **pool manifest** (`<name>.pools`) for every supervisor you start (A4.2): `pool <name> <count>` asks for
  `<count>` child ids (1 to 65536) named `<name>_0` to `<name>_<count-1>`; `tree <name> <fanout> <size>` asks for the
  two-level scheme of A4.2. Pool names are identifiers, unique in the program, and should carry your language's prefix
  (A1.1). `bees_config generate` writes the unit `bees_ids` and adds every id to `bees_atoms`.
- **A1.4** Declare which version of this contract you target. **Open:** the versioning scheme.
- **A1.5** List units in use-dependency order in the build configuration, or let `bees_config` generate it. The Silica
  compiler takes no arguments and reads its configuration from the working directory. Silica rejects a cycle of `use`
  declarations, so the generated `bees_modules` (which uses every module in the table) can be used only by a unit above
  all of them (A7.2). The trial harness (`tools/trial.mk`) runs `bees_config generate` for a leaf directory, which gives
  you the order and the generated units.

## A2. Startup and shutdown

- **A2.1** The program's `main` must **register a failure reporter before it spawns anything.** Call `bees_exit@start()`
  first: it registers the BEES listener as the reporter and starts the exit hub. Silica rejects any earlier spawn.
- **A2.2** `main` must then **start a root supervisor** and, from then on, only add actors to supervisors (A4).
- **A2.3** `main` is not an actor and has no supervisor. A program ends through Silica's `wait_for_exit` and
  `cast_exit`; your compiler decides what an exit of the root supervisor means.

## A3. Actors and scheduling

- **A3.1** Every concurrent unit of work in your language must become a Silica actor. Use a **cast-only** behaviour
  (it returns no reply) unless the actor is deliberately call-only. Do not mix the two: a cast to a call-only actor,
  or a call to a cast-only actor, is a compile error or a run-time failure of the sender.
- **A3.2** Pass a **stack policy** to every spawn: a reserve in bytes (0 means the default, the machine's memory plus
  swap) and a release algorithm. With the default reserve a program can hold only a few thousand live actors; a
  lowered reserve allows hundreds of thousands. **Open:** a recommended reserve for compiled actors.
  Also pass a **state policy** after it, `state_policy(:keep_state_area)` unless you have a reason (Silica rejects a spawn
  without one, and a supervisor child specification carries the same field). `:keep_state_area` keeps the pages an actor's
  state has grown into; the other two (`:shrink_after_compaction`, `:compact_on_request`) return them, and an actor that keeps a
  foreign buffer must use `:keep_state_area`.
- **A3.8** Write each behaviour so that Silica can **prove the old state is released.** Build the new state as a record or
  tuple literal inside the behaviour (in the returned tuple, or bound by a plain `let` and then returned), from fields of the old
  state and of the message; do not build it in a helper function, and do not take it out of a `case`. Silica then frees what
  the old state held. Otherwise it warns (W2300, "state release not proven") and copies the whole state at the end of every
  dispatch, and measured on silica-999936 that copy takes time quadratic in the number of queued messages. State that is a
  region replaced on every message cannot be proven at all; keep such an actor's message count low until Silica improves.
- **A3.3** An actor holds **no stack between messages.** Code that would suspend in the middle of a function (waiting
  for a message, sleeping, waiting for a timer) must be **split at the suspension point**: the paused computation lives
  in the actor's state, and the next message resumes it.
- **A3.4** Never block a dispatch, and never run unbounded work in one. Silica never interrupts a dispatch, and a
  running dispatch **cannot be killed** (a kill or shutdown takes effect only after it returns). Place **yield points**
  in long computations: end the dispatch and continue through a message to the actor itself. A call-only actor cannot
  yield; its work must fit one dispatch.
- **A3.5** Do not rely on unbounded recursion within one dispatch. An actor's stack is bounded by its reserve;
  exceeding it ends the actor.
- **A3.6** Placement is optional. A spawn may name a core, and `migrate_actor` moves an actor at its next dispatch
  boundary with message order kept. BEES balances actors across cores; never move an actor the program placed
  explicitly.
- **A3.7** Timers are Silica's own: `send_after(delay_ms, target, message) -> timer_ref` casts a message to an actor
  after a delay (never earlier, possibly later), `cancel_timer(timer_ref)` answers `:cancelled` or `:not_found`,
  `monotonic_time()` and `current_time()` read the clocks, and there is no `sleep`. BEES provides no timer unit. A wait
  with a timeout (a receive with `after`) is a suspension point (A3.3): arm a timer whose message carries a reference
  that identifies the wait, and **ignore any timeout whose reference is not the current wait's**, because a timeout can
  arrive after its wait has ended; cancelling the timer is an optimisation, never what makes the program correct. A
  remaining-time query is your own bookkeeping: record the deadline from `monotonic_time()` in the actor's state when
  you arm the timer. Conformance program C02 shows the pattern.

## A4. Supervision

- **A4.1** Every actor your program spawns must be a child of a supervisor. An actor you do not place under another
  supervisor must be added to the root supervisor. BEES runs no supervisors for your actors.
- **A4.2** Give every live child a **distinct child id**. Ids are symbols from a table fixed at build time, so the
  number of live children is bounded by the number of ids. The scheme is:
  1. **One pool per supervisor.** Request it with a pool manifest (A1.3a); the generated unit `bees_ids` gives
     `pool_<name>()` (the pool's number), `pool_size(pool)` and `id_of(pool, i)`, the i-th id (0 <= i < size). The same
     id is returned for the same `i` every time. An `i` outside the pool (or an unknown pool) returns the symbol
     `id_pool_exhausted`, which no pool uses: test for it and fail (A5.2).
  2. **Pools are disjoint.** Silica registers a child under its id in one program-wide namespace, so a child whose id is
     held by any live actor, in any supervisor, is refused, and the supervisor or the adder fails. Two supervisors must
     never share an id. `bees_config` guarantees it as long as every supervisor has its own pool name.
  3. **Reuse.** An id is free again once its `:temporary` child has stopped *and its supervisor has dropped the row*.
     Release an index to your allocator only after you have seen the child's end (an exit report, or a reply that shows
     it ended), never on sending the stop request. Adding a child under an id still in use fails the adder, so there is
     no probing: **each pool must have exactly one owner** (one actor, or one dispatch order) that hands out free
     indexes, for example the lowest free index first.
  4. **More live children than one pool: a tree.** `tree <name> <fanout> <size>` requests the pool `<name>_top` of
     `<fanout>` ids and `<fanout>` leaf pools `<name>_n0` to `<name>_n<fanout-1>` of `<size>` ids. Start a top supervisor
     whose children are the `<fanout>` leaf supervisors (ids from the top pool, `id_of(pool_<name>_top(), j)`); add
     workers to leaf supervisor j with ids from `leaf_<name>(j)`, the number of leaf pool j. Capacity is `fanout * size`
     live children. A deeper tree is more pools of your own naming. Spread children over leaves however you like
     (a fixed leaf per spawner, round robin); the choice is recorded in the lowering-choices file (A9).
  A supervisor whose children are supervisors has a different child shape from one whose children are workers, so a tree
  has at least two supervisor types (A4.3). Trial `trials/a03_id_pools` builds a tree of two leaves with three ids each,
  holds six live workers, and reuses an id after a stop.
- **A4.3** A supervisor is typed by one child shape (state type and behaviour type). Use one supervisor per shape, or
  one uniform actor shape for everything you compile.
- **A4.4** Choose the restart policy (`:permanent`, `:transient`, `:temporary`) and the strategy for each supervisor.
  A restarted child starts from the initial state in its child spec and gets a new identity.
- **A4.5** You may point a supervisor's report sink at the hub to receive `restarted` and `new_child`. **Open:** the hub
  reference this needs is not exported yet. The listener records every exit without it.

- **A4.6** **Finding a pid's supervisor** (needed for an exit request, A5.5). A pid carries a 64-bit identity, readable with
  `actor_id(pid)`: the high 32 bits are the **position** of the supervisor that spawned it and the low 32 bits its child
  number in that supervisor. Verified (trial `trials/a03_position_map`, Apple Silicon): all children of one supervisor
  share one position and two supervisors differ; **a supervisor's position is not the position of its own identity** (the
  position in a supervisor's own identity is its parent's), so read a supervisor's position from any child it has; a
  restarted child keeps the position and gets the next child number, and a reference to the old child does not equal
  the new one. **Silica numbers positions at run time, in the order spawners first spawn** (root supervisors started
  from `main` take 1, 2, ... in start order), so no table of positions exists at build time, `bees_config` generates
  none, and your compiler must not assume a number. What a program keeps at run time is a table from position to
  supervisor reference, filled when a supervisor is started (start it, add or find one child, read the position from the
  child's identity) and read with `actor_id(pid) shr 32`. BEES provides no such table: it is part of your compiler's output, because you write the root supervisor and know which supervisor each actor was added to. To end
  a child by pid, look up its supervisor and ask for the child by id (`:terminate_child`, which works); the supervisor's
  `:which_children` reply lists each live child's id and reference, so the id for a pid is the row whose reference
  equals the pid (that lookup is specified but not exercised by a BEES trial). `:terminate_actor`, which names the
  child by reference, is specified and not implemented. **Not verified:** whether a restarted supervisor keeps its
  position, so refresh the table entry when you see a supervisor restart.

## A5. Failure

- **A5.1** Silica has no exceptions. A failure inside an actor ends that actor, the supervisor handles it, and nothing
  inside the actor can catch it. Lower your language's recoverable-error constructs without relying on catching a
  Silica failure: use result values, or the **result-returning variants** BEES provides for common fallible
  operations. Reject at compile time any construct you cannot lower this way.
- **A5.2** End an actor on purpose with `fail_self(reason)` (a reason symbol) or `stop_self(:normal)`. Silica's own
  faults carry Silica's reasons (for example `:language_error` for a division by zero). If your language reports a
  different reason, check for the condition yourself and call `fail_self`. **`fail_self` and `stop_self` are admitted
  only directly in a behaviour function** (the function an actor is spawned with); Silica rejects them anywhere else
  (E2091). A function that the behaviour calls therefore cannot end the actor: it must return its failure to the
  behaviour (BEES's generated dispatch and id accessors return the empty reference, `:none`, or the symbol
  `id_pool_exhausted`, for exactly this reason), and the behaviour calls `fail_self`. A compiler needs one convention
  for carrying a failure up through every compiled function, and each function's caller must test it.
- **A5.3** Every branch construct you emit must be exhaustive. Silica rejects a `case` without a catch-all arm; emit an
  explicit failing arm where your language requires a failure.
- **A5.4** A `call` to a dead callee fails the caller, and a `cast` to a dead actor fails the sender, with
  `(:explicit, :actor_not_found)`. If your language treats a send to a dead recipient as harmless, **your compiler
  must lower the send so the sender survives.** BEES provides no send primitive for this and does not forbid `cast`.
  Note what a dying sender costs: the rest of its dispatch is skipped, a restart loses its state and gives it a new
  identity, its queued messages are dropped, and restarts count against the supervisor's limit.
- **A5.5** BEES provides no monitors. How links, exit signals and exit requests between actors are lowered is your
  choice. Silica can end an actor with `kill_abnormal`, which gives the reason `(:explicit, :killed)`; **open:** how to
  deliver any other reason.

## A6. Values

- **A6.1** Every value that crosses a module, actor or network boundary must be a `bees_term`. **Provisional (v0):**
  a value is a cell `(tag, n, f, a, p, h, t)` in a region; tags are nil, integer, float, symbol, actor reference,
  list cell, tuple, byte sequence and function value. The cell type is spelled in full in every signature; use the
  generated `src/shim/bees_term.silica` and do not edit it.
- **A6.2** Silica requires the recursive value type to be spelled with its tuple in full. A bare `ref?(L, normal, rec)`
  outside the tuple is rejected.
- **A6.3** **Symbols are Silica atoms and BEES has no table of its own.** Outside the generated `bees_atoms` unit, **no
  unit may write a symbol literal.** Obtain symbols from `bees_atoms` accessors, compare them with `==`, or switch on
  `bees_atoms@index(a)`. You may write a symbol pattern only for the symbols Silica itself interprets
  (`:ok`, `:normal`, `:no_reply`, restart policies, stack-policy names; the list is `FIXED_ATOMS` in
  `tools/bees_config.py`). `bees_config check` enforces this.
- **A6.4** Never create a symbol at run time. Converting text to a symbol is a lookup that fails when the program does
  not already hold the spelling. Silica has no type conversion, so converting a symbol to text, printing and encoding
  are lookups in `bees_atoms`.
- **A6.5** Any generated `case` with 512 or more literal arms fails to parse. Split large lookups (symbol tables, byte
  tables, module-table dispatch) into helper functions of at most 256 arms, as `bees_config` does.
- **A6.6** Integers are `int64`; overflow must fail the actor. Larger integers wait on Silica.
- **A6.7** A byte sequence is a `buf(uint8)` plus a bit length, never a Silica string. A `buf` may be a message only
  when the region it lives in is sent with it. **Provisional:** v0 stores a byte sequence as a list of byte cells.
  Outside a foreign function, **every function that takes or returns a `buf(L, ...)` must also take or return the
  `region(L, ...)` it lives in** in the same signature (a parameter, a record field or a tuple element); Silica rejects it
  otherwise (E2323). Pass the region down with the buffer.
- **A6.8** Bit-level and byte-level operations are yours. Silica has no type conversion, and its bitwise operators take
  `uint64`. Generate lookups (for example a 256-way `case` from a byte to the matching literal) and combine them with
  same-type arithmetic. Literal bytes, strings and numbers become bytes at compile time.
- **A6.9** A message is a record that carries its region: `{ r: region(L, normal), c: <value> }`. Name every value
  lifetime `L` and type every region that carries values `region(L, normal)`. Build the message in a function that
  returns it, once per send, and bind a computed message to a name before casting it; do not pass a computed record or
  call inline as the message.
- **A6.10** Constructors and accessors return a single reference, not a record or tuple, and the heap is a record
  `{ r: region(L, normal) }` passed in and kept in the actor state.
- **A6.11** More than 8 parameters must be packed, because Silica allows 8.
- **A6.12** A function that builds a record literal must declare `mem(normal)`; every effect a sequence declares must be
  used, and every effect it uses must be declared.

## A7. Dynamic dispatch

- **A7.1** Calls whose target is computed at run time (`apply`, calls through function values) go through the
  program-wide **module table**, the generated unit `bees_modules`, which `bees_config` builds from the `.module`
  manifests (A1.3). Statically known calls stay ordinary Silica calls. You may write your own dispatch instead; say so
  in the lowering-choices file.
- **A7.2** The **calling convention** is fixed, so the table is a plain `case` and needs no function pointers by name:
  - an entry `<fn>` is `fn <fn>(ap: APPLY, h: HEAP, args: TERM) -> TERM`, where `args` is a list value of exactly
    `<arity>` values and the result is one value;
  - a function-value body `<fn>` is `fn <fn>(ap: APPLY, h: HEAP, env: TERM, args: TERM) -> TERM`, where `env` is the list
    of values the function value captured;
  - HEAP is the heap record `{ r: region(L, normal) }`, TERM the value cell reference of `bees_term`, and
    `APPLY = fn(HEAP, TERM, TERM) -> TERM`, the type of the generated `bees_modules@dispatch`. More than 8 source
    parameters are packed into the list (A6.11), so every entry has the same shape.
  - **Silica forbids cyclic `use`, so no module in the table can use `bees_modules`.** The table passes itself, as the
    function value `dispatch`, to every entry and every function-value body as `ap`. A function that must apply
    dynamically takes `ap` as a parameter, passes it down to the functions that may apply dynamically, and calls
    `ap(h, target, args)`. Only the program's top unit (the one with `main`) names `bees_modules`, and passes
    `bees_modules@dispatch` into the first function that needs it (a function can be passed as a value, trial
    `trials/a03_module_table`). Silica passes lifetime-polymorphic function values without difficulty.
- **A7.3** What `bees_modules` provides (all with the heap `h` first where a value is built):
  - `dispatch(h, target, args)`: `target` is a function value (call it) or a 2-tuple value `{Module, Function}` (apply it);
  - `apply(h, m, f, args)`: apply module symbol `m`, function symbol `f` (arity is the length of `args`);
  - `apply_fun(h, fv, args)`, and `fun_of(h, m, id, env)`, which builds the function value for fun `id` of module `m`
    capturing `env`. A function value is the cell kind 8 of `bees_term`; its first number is the module's index, which
    `fun_of` takes from `module_index(m)`, so a compiler never writes a module index;
  - `is_exported(m, f, arity)`, `has_module(m)`, `module_index(m)` (-1 when absent) and `module_count()`.
  An unknown module, function or arity, a value that is not a function value or tuple, or an unknown fun id gives the
  empty reference (`:none`; test it with `bees_term@is_none`). The table cannot end the actor (A5.2), so the caller fails
  with `fail_self(bees_atoms@a_undef())` for a missing function and `fail_self(bees_atoms@a_badfun())` for a bad function
  value; `bees_config` puts both symbols into `bees_atoms` whenever a module manifest exists.
- **A7.4** The dispatch tiers itself: no `case` in the generated unit has more than 256 arms, so a module table of any
  size compiles (A6.5). Trial `trials/a03_module_table` has a module with 300 entries.

## A8. Foreign code and untrusted input

- **A8.1** Foreign-function calls live in a `dangerous_`-prefixed module and run in a worker actor created with
  `spawn_dangerous`. The declarations, the worker and its spawn site were required to be in one unit on the previous
  compiler; not re-verified on this one.
- **A8.2** Data returned by foreign code is tainted. It reaches a BEES program only through **re-creation**: a
  validated copy built in a fresh region. **Update 2026-11-06:** the language's derived `decode((:etf), frame)` (which replaced `recreate`; the marker traits `Recreatable` and `Transportable` are gone) and `encode((:etf), value)` are callable on `silica-999935` (SD-32 resolved there). **The required design for BEES (user ruling) is that the decode, and the encode, each happen in the `sequence` of a `sequence ... produces pure ... end` block, so no tainted value crosses an actor boundary or a cast.** The language's own `transport_beam_demo` does this; whether it passes the taint checker for bytes that came from a carrier in BEES's own actor shapes is **untested by BEES** (milestone N0.1). BEES's own receive step is still a stub behind one function (`bees_ingress@recreate`) until N0.0 ports it; a compiler author's programs get the language's calls directly.
- **A8.3** Each dangerous actor is an operating-system thread. Pool them.

## A9. What you must document for your own users

- **A9.1** Your compiler must write a **lowering-choices file** for every program it compiles (section 0). The format is
  `contract/conformance/lowering-choices.md`: one line for each construct the contract leaves to you, each naming the
  requirement it answers, with one of the listed choices. The entries are: stack reserve (A3.2), suspension points
  (A3.3), yield points (A3.4), child-id scheme and supervisor tree (A4.2), supervisor shape (A4.3), restart policy and
  strategy (A4.4), recoverable-error constructs (A5.1), sends to dead recipients (A5.4), links and exit requests (A5.5),
  byte and bit operations (A6.8) and dynamic dispatch (A7.1). `tools/check_lowering_choices.py FILE` must accept the file.
- **A9.2** Your compiler's own documentation must state, in the language your users read, how it lowered the same
  constructs, including what a send to a dead recipient costs them (A5.4).

## A10. Conformance

- **A10.1** Your compiler conforms when the reference programs of the conformance kit, `contract/conformance/programs`
  (C01 to C08), written in your language and compiled by it, build and run on BEES with the expected output, and your
  lowering-choices file passes its checker (A9.1). The programs are: a message exchange that suspends in the middle of a
  function and resumes (C01), a receive with a timeout (C02), a fallible call rewritten to its result-returning form
  (C03), function values and dynamic application (C04), binary matching (C05), a ring of actors passing a token (C06),
  a supervised actor that fails and is restarted from its initial state (C07), and every kind of actor end counted by
  the exit hub (C08).
- **A10.2** Run one program with `tools/conformance.py run LEAF ENTRY C02`. `contract/conformance/README.md` says what a
  pass means, how the output is filtered and how to build a leaf. Each program has a hand-written reference lowering
  in Silica that passes today; read it as an example, not as the only answer.

---

# Part B. What BEES provides

## B1. Available now (version 0, may change)

| Unit or tool | Provides |
| --- | --- |
| `bees_term` | Value cells: constructors, accessors, list and tuple helpers, equality, copy into another region. Generated by `tools/gen_bees_term.py`. |
| `bees_recv` | A save queue, for code that must skip messages and come back to them. |
| `bees_atoms` | The generated symbol lookups: one accessor per symbol, `spelling`, `from_spelling`, `index`, `count`, tiered above 256 symbols. |
| `bees_exit` | The listener (registered as the FailureReporter) and the exit hub. The listener parses every failure report for every ended actor, supervised or not, into a record (identity, agent type, reason, reason tag, supervisor, first frame). The hub counts by reason. |
| `bees_reporter` | A plain reporter that prints every failure, for tests. |
| `bees_config` | `generate`: from your manifests, `bees_atoms` (symbols), `bees_modules` (the module table, A7), `bees_ids` (child-id pools, A4.2) and, when `.wire` manifests exist, the wire codec units, all sorted, byte-identical on every run and tiered at 256 arms; `check`: no unit writes a symbol literal. |
| `bees_modules`, `bees_ids` | Generated, never edited, never checked in: dispatch by module, function and arity, by function value and by `{Module, Function}`; child-id pools and trees. |
| `bees_wire`, `bees_wire_tables`, `bees_wire_msgs` | The typed message codec: ETF, as `term_to_binary/1` writes it, for the typed subset in `contract/wire-v1.md` section 5. `bees_wire` is hand-written (bounds-checked readers and writers, the limits, the sixteen rejection atoms). `bees_wire_tables` and `bees_wire_msgs` are generated by `bees_config wire` (and by `generate`) from `<unit>.wire` manifests, one line per message type: `message <name> <silica type>` (or implied by the `remote` and `local` lines of the node layer, B1a). Per message they hold an encoder `enc_<name>`, a decoder `dec_<name>`, and a validating dispatcher by registered name. A message type with a field the codec does not carry (actor references, regions and references, `buf`, functions, sum types, tagged tuples, standard data structures) is a build error. **Interim:** Silica is designing `encode`/`decode((:etf), ...)` as language features; when they are in the compiler this codec goes and the bytes stay the same. **Code ported 2026-11-09, built and run 2026-11-10 on silica-999926 (see [silica-transport-alignment.md](silica-transport-alignment.md) and the 2026-11-09 and 2026-11-10 sections of [silica-defects.md](silica-defects.md)):** a node program no longer uses them: its messages are encoded and decoded by the language (`encode`/`decode((:etf), ...)`) through the generated `bees_msgs` (`enc_<name>`, `dec_<name>`, `validate_named`); the typed codec is generated only for manifests without node lines (the `m1_wire_*` trials, the oracle). |
| `bees_dist`, `dangerous_bees_net`, `bees_ingress`, generated `bees_peers`, the TCP carrier | The node layer: the Erlang distribution handshake (version 6, no digest), 4-byte framing, net ticks, the one control message `REG_SEND`, a peer table, a proxy actor per remote name and a deliverer per local name. Profile: `contract/wire-v1.md`. What it gives you and what you still owe: section B1a. **Test-only: no authentication, no encryption, `127.0.0.1`, one link per node, no reconnect.** **Code ported 2026-11-09, built and run 2026-11-10 on silica-999926 (see [silica-transport-alignment.md](silica-transport-alignment.md) and the 2026-11-09 and 2026-11-10 sections of [silica-defects.md](silica-defects.md)):** the carrier is the language's `(:tcp)` carrier (`dangerous_tcp_carrier`, spawned by the root unit's `carrier_new()`); `dangerous_bees_net` is the receive actor (`conn`) and the send actor (`tx`) of mvp.md 3.3 over the carrier contract; `bees_dist` works over strings; the generated `bees_msgs` holds the codecs. |
| Trial harness | `tools/trial.mk`: builds, runs and compares leaf directories against `.scout` goldens. |
| Reference lowerings | `trials/s09_reference_lowerings` (selective receive, receive with a timeout, a fallible call rewritten to its result-returning form, function values and dynamic apply, byte matching) and `trials/a02_ring` (a ring and a supervised restart). Generator trials: `trials/a03_module_table`, `trials/a03_id_pools` and `trials/a03_position_map`. |
| Conformance kit | `contract/conformance`: eight reference programs with expected output and passing lowerings, the lowering-choices format, `tools/conformance.py` and `tools/check_lowering_choices.py`. |

## B1a. The node layer: sending to a name on another node (version 0)

**Status:** works between two BEES programs on one machine (milestones M3 and M4, trials `trials/m3_dist` and
`trials/m4_demo`). **It is test-only**: no authentication and no encryption (every program prints a banner saying so), `127.0.0.1`
only, macOS Apple Silicon only. The wire it speaks is `contract/wire-v1.md`; read that for bytes. This section says what
the layer does for a compiler and what the compiler must still do. Every statement is **provisional** unless it says
otherwise.

**What you get.** Your compiled program can `cast_registered(:name, msg impl ActorMessage {})` to a registered name that
lives in **another program** (another operating-system process, here a node), with the same Silica code you would write for a
local name. Nothing in the source mentions the network.

**N1. The node manifest.** Put these lines into a `<unit>.wire` manifest (the same file type as the `message` lines of A1.2;
`bees_config generate` reads them and writes `bees_peers`, the codec units and `bees_atoms` entries):

| Line | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `node <name>` | this program's node name: ASCII letters, digits, `_ . @ -`, at most 255 bytes, for example `b@127.0.0.1`. **Required.** |
| `creation <n>` | optional, 0 to 4294967295, default 1. A constant written into the handshake and into the sender's pid; the peer does not check it. **Your compiler chooses it** (BEES does not assign or increment it). |
| `timing <open_ms> <io_ms> <tick_ms>` | optional, defaults 10000 60000 15000, each 1 to 60000 (`tick_ms` may be 0). `open_ms` bounds listening, accepting and connecting; a peer that sends nothing for `io_ms` is lost; a node that has written nothing for `tick_ms` sends a net tick. `tick_ms` 0 sends none (a test setting: the peer will drop you). Read the three values back with `bees_peers@open_ms()`, `io_ms()`, `tick_ms()`. |
| `peer <name> <host> <port> <listen\|dial>` | a node this program may talk to. `<host>` must be `127.0.0.1`. **The first `peer` line is the program's one link**: `dial` connects to it, `listen` binds the port and accepts one connection, which must name a listed node. Other `peer` lines are table entries (names that may dial in). At least one `peer` line is required. |
| `remote <name> @ <peer> cast <type>` | a registered name that lives on `<peer>`. `bees_config` generates a **proxy actor**, registered under `<name>` on this node, whose message type is `<type>`. Your code casts to `<name>` exactly as to a local actor. |
| `local <name> cast <type>` | a registered name on this node that the peer may cast to. `bees_config` generates the decoder and a short-lived deliverer that `cast_registered`s the decoded value to `<name>`. **Your program must register an actor under that name** (A4.1 still applies). |
| `message <name> <type>` | a message type with no node line, for the codec alone (as before). |

`<name>` is `[a-z][a-z0-9_]*`. At most 16 `remote` and 16 `local` lines. A name cannot be both, or listed twice, and a
`remote` must name a listed `peer` (`bees_config` rejects the manifest with `file:line: message`). `<type>` is Silica's own
type text, restricted to the typed subset (`contract/wire-v1.md` section 5.3): the integer widths, `float32`, `float64`,
`boolean`, `char`, `atom`, `string`, tuples of two or more, records of one or more fields, and `List[T]`. Anything else is a
build error that names the message, the field path and the type. **Keep each record to two to four fields and group
larger messages into nested records**: a flat record of 22 fields did not compile in 300 s (SD-36). A frame is at most 4096
bytes and a payload at most 4000, and text is ASCII.

**N2. What the compiler must write.** The node layer is a set of units plus two things only your compiler can write:

- **N2.1** The program's **root unit must be named `dangerous_*` and must contain the carrier's edge section**: the carrier is
  the language's `(:tcp)` carrier, a Fifi wrapper, so every program that depends on it carries the prefix (FFI wrapper
  specification 3.1). `tools/bees_edge_gen.py NAME OUT --use bees_msgs --use bees_dist --use dangerous_bees_net --use bees_peers ROLE_FILES...`
  writes that unit from `src/shim/bees_tcp_edge.part` (one function, `carrier_new()`, which spawns the stdlib's
  `dangerous_tcp_carrier`), `src/shim/bees_node_edge.part` (the node's startup, N2.2) and your own code; its header names
  `carrier`, `wireframe`, `dangerous_sockets` and `dangerous_tcp_carrier`, and your
  leaf's `lib/` must link those stdlib units plus `wireframe` and `wire_etf` (see `trials/m3_dist/nodes/a/lib`), with the socket
  wrappers' archive and sidecar under `dangerous_exposure_source` (`make native`). The Makefiles of `trials/m3_dist/nodes/a` and
  `trials/m4_demo/nodes/a` are the worked examples. (Ported 2026-11-09; built and run 2026-11-10 on silica-999926.)
- **N2.2** The node's **startup**, which no tool writes yet: create the carrier for the one link and start the node, as
  `node_start` does in `trials/m3_dist/roles/node.role`: `c <- carrier_new(); n <- net_start(c, bees_peers@io_ms(),
  bees_peers@tick_ms())`. `net_start` and `net_launch` are not in `dangerous_bees_net`: they are in `src/shim/bees_node_edge.part`,
  which `bees_edge_gen.py` pastes into the root unit when `--use dangerous_bees_net` is given, because `dangerous_bees_net` holds the
  carrier as a `dangerous_actor_ref` and so must carry the `dangerous_` prefix (E4026), and a call to any function of a `dangerous_`
  unit is allowed only inside an FFI worker (E4042). The root unit therefore spawns `dangerous_bees_net`'s behaviours by reference
  and casts to them. `net_start` prints the test-only banner; on a dialing node it starts the writer, the proxies and a reaper,
  spawns the connection actor and opens the carrier with `(:open, conn, bees_peers@link_address())` (`"host:port"`); on a listening
  node it spawns the listen actor `lsn` and opens the carrier with `"listen:port"` (127.0.0.1), and `lsn` starts the writer, the
  proxies and the connection actor on the first accepted connection. `net_launch(c, io_ms, tick_ms)` does the same and also
  returns the writer (on a dialing node; on a listening node there is none until a peer is accepted). Verified 2026-11-10 on
  silica-999926: `trials/m3_dist` and `trials/m4_demo` build and pass.
- **N2.3** **Register the receiver** under each `local` name with `spawn_registered` and a behaviour whose message type is the
  `local` line's type. If nothing holds the name when a frame arrives, the **deliverer** (a short-lived actor) fails, not the
  connection (SD-33); BEES cannot count that, it is visible only as a failure report.
- **N2.4** **Supervise every actor the node layer spawns** (A4.1): the connection actor, the writer, the proxies, the reaper,
  the per-frame assemblers and the deliverers. **Open:** `dangerous_bees_net` and the generated `bees_peers` spawn them plainly today (the
  trials run under the runtime's root supervisor); a supervised variant that takes your supervisor and child ids from your
  pool does not exist. Until it does, say in your lowering-choices file (A9.1) that you did not supervise them.
- **N2.5** Everything in A1 to A10 still applies to your own units.

**N3. Failure, as your program sees it.** Failure maps onto Silica's own rules (A5.4); the layer adds no new failure kind.

- When the link ends (the peer closes, is killed, goes silent for `io_ms`, or breaks the framing), every proxy is **ended**
  with `kill_abnormal`. A `cast_registered` to the name then **fails the sender** with `(:explicit, :actor_not_found)`, the
  report Silica gives for any dead actor. **The name is gone for good: there is no reconnect**, so every later cast fails
  the sender again, and a supervisor that restarts the sender gets the same failure until the program restarts.
- Your compiler must lower a send to a remote name the way it lowers a send to a possibly dead actor (A5.4). **A service
  that answers a client by casting to a `reply_to` name dies when the client's node is gone**, because on the service's node
  that name is a proxy that has ended. This was argued, not run. Lower such sends so the sender survives if your language
  needs that.
- A frame the peer sends that the layer refuses (a pid from another node, an unknown or unserved target, a payload that
  fails its type) is dropped and audited, and the link stays up; a framing violation closes the link. Audit lines are
  `[bees audit] <kind> <who> <n>` on standard output.

**N4. Replies.** There is no call across nodes (a Silica call returns at the end of the callee's dispatch, and foreign results
reach an actor as casts). Put a `reply_to` field of type `atom` in the request and have the service `cast_registered` its
answer to that name; on the service's node that name must be a `remote` line for a name on the client's node, and on the
client's node a `local` line.

**N5. What the compiler must still do itself.** BEES's node layer is deliberately small.

- **Terms of any shape are yours.** The codec carries typed values only. A dynamic language lowers its values to a typed
  message (a record of known fields, a tag atom the program holds plus a payload, a byte list) or to its own encoding in a
  `string`; BEES provides no any-type codec and Silica does not support one.
- **Pids, links, monitors, remote spawn, `nodedown`, `net_kernel`, `global`, `pg`** are not provided. A send is to a
  **registered name**, not a pid; the pid on the wire is the proxy's index and is only checked for its node.
- **Reconnect, backoff, discovery and EPMD** are yours or later; there is none.
- **Node names and creations** are yours. The peer table is fixed at build time (D16): a program cannot talk to a node it
  does not list.
- **Timers** are Silica's (A3.3); BEES's ticks use them internally and you do not have to.
- **Bytes and the host** (files, other transports, DNS) are yours. The carrier is BEES's own foreign-function code and is not
  exposed to your program.
- **One compiler per application:** every program of one application is built by one compiler, so the manifests of its nodes
  agree. BEES checks nothing across programs; a type mismatch shows up as a refused frame.
- **Security.** Treat the link as untrusted and the layer as test-only: there is no authentication and no encryption until
  BEAM mode's cookie (N2) or TRUST (N3 to N5, a separate implementation with its own TLS) exists, and the receive step in BEES's code is a stub (A8.2) whose protection is BEES's own validation, not the language's taint
  guarantee. A program that must be secure must not claim it on this layer. Keep a person in the loop (section 0).
- **Interoperating with a stock Erlang node is not possible** with this layer today (no cookie digest). **Decided 2026-11-06 (roadmap D36): BEAM mode will use Erlang's cookie authentication (milestone N2, with EPMD and a live test against `erl -sname`)**; TRUST is a separate protocol and cannot talk to a stock node.

## B1b. `bees.config` versus the manifest (design; nothing is implemented)

BEES's inter-node layer will read one configuration file, **`bees.config`** (Erlang term text, read by BEES's own reader; roadmap D37;
the full specification is [development-plan/bees-config-file.md](../development-plan/bees-config-file.md)). It chooses the
mode, `beam` or `trust` (two separate implementations, D36; one per node; the default is `trust`), and carries every option of both. It
**replaces `sys.config`**: BEES reads no `sys.config`. What a compiler author puts where:

| Where | What |
| --- | --- |
| The **manifest** (`<unit>.wire`, N1 above) | The build-time schema: `node` (the name, which becomes an atom), `creation` (default), `timing` (defaults), `peer` names, `remote` and `local` names with their types, `message` types. The generated code depends on these. |
| **`bees.config`** | Everything an operator changes without a rebuild: `mode`, addresses and ports, the cookie file, certificates, keys, the whitelist and pins files, limits and timeouts. Where both can say a value, `bees.config` wins; a node name or peer name that differs from the manifest's is a boot error (D16). |

Four rulings of 2026-11-06 matter to a compiler author: **the default mode is `trust`** (ruled); **`listen_address` has no
default** and must be written in the section of the selected mode (the trials write `127.0.0.1`); **the frame and argument caps
are the same as BEAM's** (4294967295 bytes; the build implements 4096 until N1, a larger value is a boot error "not built yet", never
clamped; the limits are in [bees-config-file.md](../development-plan/bees-config-file.md) section 5.4); and a `trust` node whose
**whitelist file is configured but missing or unreadable fails to boot with a clear message** (it never runs silently as
standalone). How TRUST's any-type `args` and result are handled is **open: under discussion with the user**; terms of any shape are the
compiler's, not BEES's.

A compiler ships `bees.config` with the program, or, for a target with no file system (the ESP32-S3), compiles it and every file it names
into a generated Silica module that BEES's reader reads (D26; the module's shape is a contract item not yet fixed). The compiler never needs to write
or edit the file. A program whose manifest has `remote` or `local` lines is a BEAM-mode program and needs `{mode, beam}`.

Two rules apply to every program that crosses a node boundary, in both modes (user rulings 2026-11-06; **required design, not shown to work for carrier bytes in BEES's code**): conversion between typed values and bytes is done in the `sequence` of a `sequence ... produces pure` block, and a connection has one send actor and one separate receive actor (development-plan/mvp.md sections 3.3 and 4).

## B2. Planned

| Item | Status |
| --- | --- |
| Contract versioning scheme (A1.4) | planned |
| A run-time table from position to supervisor (A4.6), and actor identity helpers | planned (no build-time part exists) |
| Registered names, process-information queries | planned |
| Result-returning variants of common fallible library calls | planned |
| In-memory tables, counters, persistent storage of values | planned |
| Host input and output, files, transports and DNS (wrappers over Silica's foreign-function interface) | planned |
| Re-creation of foreign data | blocked on Silica |
| Balancing and placement of actors across cores | planned |
| Secure inter-node communication (TRUST: a separate implementation from BEAM mode, D36) | planned (N3 to N5); needs a TLS engine, which needs the user's explicit approval (D38). The unauthenticated BEAM-mode node layer exists (B1a) |
| The BEES configuration file `bees.config` (D37) | designed (B1b, [development-plan/bees-config-file.md](../development-plan/bees-config-file.md)); not built (N0) |
| Reconnect, more than one link per node, pids and links across nodes, stock Erlang interoperation | planned, none built |
| Encoding and decoding of values for a wire (ETF), framing and transports | Silica is designing these as language features (`Transportable`, `encode`/`decode`, a carrier actor contract); BEES leaves typed values to them when they exist and supplies the distribution layer and foreign pids above them (terms of any shape are the compiler's, not BEES's). Until then BEES ships its own interim codec (B1) |

## B3. Not provided (yours or Silica's)

| Item | Owner |
| --- | --- |
| A language's syntax, types, semantics and standard library | Your compiler |
| Lowering of sends to dead recipients, links, exit requests, recoverable errors | Your compiler |
| Bit-level and byte-level operations, large integers | Your compiler (large integers also wait on Silica) |
| Timers, the clocks, and remaining-time queries | Timers and clocks are Silica's own (A3.7); remaining time is your compiler's, from a deadline it records |
| Monitors | Not part of BEES |
| State-machine actors, a registry that can name an actor after it starts, links and monitors in the runtime | Silica, not delivered yet |

# Part C. Open points

1. The contract's versioning scheme (A1.4). The manifest and module-table formats (A1.3, A7) and the child-id scheme
   (A4.2) are decided.
2. A recommended stack reserve for compiled actors (A3.2); a way to give a supervisor child an id without a fixed pool
   (Silica would have to allow it); whether a restarted supervisor keeps its position (A4.6).
3. Delivering exit reasons other than `(:explicit, :killed)` (A5.5), and a non-failing send (A5.4).
4. A structured failure report from Silica. The listener reads the text of Silica's report today, so a change to that
   text breaks it.
5. One failure listener handles about 20,000 reports per second; beyond that its queue grows. Faster parsing or parallel
   workers are planned.
6. A supervised cast-only actor that holds a region and an actor reference and casts from inside its dispatch fails on its
   second message; avoid that shape until it is fixed.
7. Targets other than Apple Silicon macOS are unverified.
8. The node layer (B1a): a supervised start that takes your supervisor and ids (N2.4); a generated startup (N2.2); a
   non-failing send to a remote name (N3); reconnect; more than one link per node; TRUST's TLS; the receive step as
   the language's `decode` instead of the stub (A8.2, N0.0); whether to add the OTP 25 digest shorthand flag
   (`0x400_0000`) to the flag set (`contract/wire-v1.md` section 3.3).

# Part D. If your language is a BEAM language

The same requirements apply. The extra constructs (selective receive, `gen_server`, `supervisor` and `gen_statem`
modules, NIFs, binaries and bit syntax, remote procedure calls) will be covered by a BEAM-language supplement to this
document; until it is published, apply Part A to them and record your lowering in the lowering-choices file.
